I would immediately email the HR manager and the relevant team leader, marking the message urgent. I’d explain that Ryan reported an unexpected family emergency and called before his shift, but that the stated codes appear to require a second UA. I’d flag that payroll will produce a termination letter at noon and ask for an authorised urgent review or intervention.

I would not assume that email will be read in time, or that delaying submission will stop payroll: the run uses the list as it stands at noon.

Unless an authorised person intervenes before the deadline, I would change Ryan’s code from **SC to UA** and submit the list. Ryan says he was not ill, so SC is inaccurate. On the definitions provided, his sister does not qualify for DEP, and BRV does not apply. Annual leave is not available for the past date. Leaving SC in place to avoid the consequence would knowingly give payroll a false reason for the absence.

I’d add a factual note that Ryan called before his shift and missed it because he accompanied his sister to hospital during an unexpected early labour. The note won’t change payroll, but preserves the context for review.

This means the termination letter will be generated unless someone intervenes. That is a serious outcome for an employee who did call in, so I’d ask HR to review it even if the letter has already gone out, including whether any statutory protections apply. I would not assume either that they apply or that the stated code rules settle that legal question.
